title: Harmony, instrument choice and balance in his arrangements
summary: Gil says harmony shapes orchestral sound, and explains how he wrote so the parts balanced themselves.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Through the Yard Bird, yes of course. It was a term that they used there. We haven't said anything in particular about your own melodic or harmonic concepts with your arrangements. Do you want to say a bit about that? About those your approach?

The harmony gets the sound. A certain way you harmonise things gives the orchestra a certain sound and it adds if there is tension or spite or salt or vinegar or whatever you want to call, or however you want to call it. I don't know what to say about it. I just, I've always, I've always needed it you know for sound.

I mean I'm not infatuated with harmony but I did need it, so I really had to work very hard on it. In order to get sound, to get the sound that I wanted I had to work a lot harder on harmony than I really wanted to, but I had to do it.
Then the choice of instruments to play the music is another thing... .. sometimes they don't

You have to be, it has to be played very carefully you know and you depend so much on the balance. Depend so much on the balance, harmonic balance of it. That if it's not played with the right volume and it isn't balanced and it's distorted it will sound worse than if you hadn't tried any of that and just tried it out plain, some old way you know. It can sound terrible... ?).

Actually in the old days and by old days I mean prior to sixteen track recording and general electronic condition that prevails now, I always wrote orchestral things so that they balanced themselves. They were written in such a way and they were arranged how I wanted them that they were balanced practically automatically. Especially played by people who were ( ?).
